papers_read.title_as_printed: Multimodal Convolutional Mixer for Mild Cognitive Impairment Detection (Grigas, Damasevicius, Maskeliunas; Comput Mater Contin 2025)
Tortuosity and discrete compactness biomarkers for machine learning-based classification of mild cognitive impairment (Torres Guzman et al.; Biomed Signal Process Control 2026)

what_each_reports.P-359: CN vs MCI, MCM-768 on the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) dataset only, sagittal plane, 85/15 random split: accuracy 0.9639, sensitivity 0.9690, specificity 0.9587 (Table 4). On the pooled ADNI+MCSA+OASIS3 set the best sagittal accuracy is 0.9492 (Table 7); averaged over planes 0.9228 (Table 10). Inputs are fused T1w MRI + PiB-PET mid-slices concatenated with MMSE, CDR, FAQ, education, gender and blood pressure.
what_each_reports.P-125: HC vs MCI, 74 ADNI subjects (37/37), 8 amygdala morphometric features (volume, normalised volume, discrete compactness, tortuosity per hemisphere), 60/40 split: abstract states test accuracy 82.14%; the results section and Table 6 give mean test accuracy 80.00 +/- 2.43% (RF), 79.29% (SVM), 77.86% (KNN), 80.00% (ANN); test AUC 85.71-90.31%.

quantity_a: Accuracy of CN-vs-MCI classification in MCSA (sagittal slice) from a multimodal model whose inputs include the clinical instruments (CDR, MMSE, FAQ) used to define the diagnostic labels, plus PiB-PET and T1w MRI; random 85/15 hold-out.
quantity_b: Accuracy of HC-vs-MCI classification in 74 ADNI subjects from 8 FreeSurfer amygdala shape/volume features only (structural MRI); 60/40 hold-out.
incompatible_if_same: No. Two different methods on different inputs each report their own score; neither paper claims an ordering that the other refutes (P-125 does not test multimodal models; P-359 does not test amygdala morphometry). A higher accuracy for a richer predictor set is not a contradiction.

gates.task: match: both CN/HC vs MCI detection (T1).
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: P-359's 96.3% is MCSA-only ('Classification results using only MCSA dataset sagittal plane'); its pooled result mixes MCSA, OASIS3 and 27/27 ADNI subjects. P-125 is ADNI only. No waiver on record.
gates.validation_tier: match: both internal hold-out (V2); P-359 also reports LODO only in a figure.
gates.modality_family: mismatch: P-359 is multimodal (T1w MRI + PiB amyloid PET + cognitive tests + clinical/demographic); P-125 is structural MRI morphometry only. The record's 'structural_mri' for both is wrong for P-359.

endpoint_and_metric: compatible metric type (accuracy vs accuracy) but incompatible predictor set and label circularity: P-359 feeds CDR/MMSE/FAQ, the instruments that define MCI, into the classifier, and its ablation shows removing cognitive tests produces the largest accuracy drop.
performance_validity: flag does not apply by the automatic test: 0.9639 is below 0.97 and the MCSA arm has 824 subjects; however it is internal random-split validation with no external cohort, and the comparison is a performance comparison.
independence: Distinct studies, no shared authors. Both draw on ADNI but P-359 uses only 27/27 ADNI subjects and its headline figure uses none.
grounds: The contested 96.3% is an MCSA-only result, so the dataset-family gate fails against P-125's ADNI-only cohort, with no waiver on record.

P-359's predictor set is multimodal and includes the diagnostic instruments (CDR, MMSE, FAQ), whereas P-125 uses eight amygdala morphometric features, so the modality family and input representation differ (the C-80 precedent).
Even if set side by side, neither study claims an ordering the other refutes; the two accuracies are different methods' scores, not incompatible estimates of one quantity.

evidence_quotes.quote: achieves a classification accuracy of 96.3% on the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) dataset (sagittal plane), outperforming state-of-the-art models by 5%-20%.
It was nonsensical to assess the ADNI and OASIS3 separately due to their size.
Removing cognitive test features (MMSE, CDR, and FAQ) results in the highest drop in accuracy
The analysis included a total of 74 participants, comprising 37 healthy control subjects and 37 mild cognitive impairment patients. Imaging data were sourced from the ADNI database.
The mean test accuracy was 80.00 +/- 2.43 %, 79.29 +/- 5.78 %, 77.86 +/- 3.71 % and 80.00 +/- 3.97 % for the RF, SVM, KNN and ANN models respectively.

record_defects: dataset_equal 'Yes' (implying ADNI for both) is wrong: P-359's 96.3% comes from MCSA only.
modality_family 'structural_mri' is wrong for P-359, which fuses PiB-PET with T1w MRI and adds cognitive, clinical and demographic features.
The pack registry Best_Metric 'Acc 89.1' for P-359 does not match any accuracy in the paper; 89.1% is the full-dataset sensitivity (abstract).
P-125's 82.14% is the abstract figure; the paper's own Table 6 reports best mean test accuracy 80.00%, an internal inconsistency in the source that the record does not note.
The record's resolution_status 'partially_resolved_candidate' rests on a list of third papers that merely report other accuracies; none shows a condition separating these two results.
what_would_change_the_verdict: An ADNI-only, MRI-only result from P-359 on the same CN-vs-MCI comparison with an interval excluding P-125's estimate would make the quantities comparable; even then, both being method scores with no refuted ordering would make it a false positive rather than genuine.
